old_title: Iran war live: Vance says 'things happen' after US accused of wedding strike
new_title: Iran war live: Tehran attacks ships in Hormuz after US strikes Iranian oil tankers
old_text:
JD Vance has faced backlash after appearing to dismiss reports that a US strike killed five people, including two children, at a wedding gathering in southern Iran.
When asked about whether a US strike was responsible, he said "sometimes things happen".
He said: "I will say that the Iranian state media has not been a very good scribe about what's happened in the conflict thus far, so I'm extremely sceptical of this."
The toll was confirmed not by the Iranian government but by the Iranian Red Crescent, a member of the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement.
"What I can say with 100% confidence is that, unlike the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] IRGC, the United States never targets civilians in combat," Vance said. "We never will do that. We never have done that, and unfortunately, obviously, sometimes things happen."
Meanwhile, president Donald Trump insisted he had done the "right thing" with the war.
It comes amid fears Trump is planning to extend Washington's war on Iran, after The Wall Street Journal reported that the Pentagon was extending the presence of troops in the Middle East into next year.
We are pausing our coverage for now
We are pausing our coverage on the Iran war for now.
Trump to use $400M Qatari gift plane for international trips despite security concerns
President Donald Trump plans to fly to Ireland next week on the Boeing 747 donated by Qatar, despite concerns over its security and unfinished upgrades, a senior White House official told the Washington Post.
The trip will mark Trump's first international journey on the Qatari jet since U.S. officials secretly moved him to another plane during his return from July's NATO summit in Turkey after intelligence indicated a potential Iranian threat.
"We don't comment on specific upgrades or modifications to Air Force One," a senior administration official told the Post. "We maintain a consistent posture that ensures a safe, secure, and reliable capability for the President of the United States and routinely evolve the capability as required to maintain that posture."
Comment: Trump doesn't understand the forever war he's created with Iran
Trump remains mesmerized by Putin even as the Kremlin helps Iran kill Americans and weaken US influence around the globe, explains world affairs editor Sam Kiley:
'Sometimes things happen': Vance addresses suspected US strike on Iranian wedding
Explained: Evidence points to US weapon in deadly strike on Iran wedding celebration
The United States is investigating a deadly strike on a wedding gathering in southern Iran after weapons experts reviewing verified images and video concluded the blast was likely caused by a direct hit from a U.S. munition, Vice President JD Vance said Thursday.
Five people have died following Tuesday's strike on a home hosting the celebration, according to Iranian state television, which reported Thursday that a 22-year-old woman had died from her injuries. Iranian officials said nearly 70 others were wounded.
The Trump administration has not accepted responsibility for the strike, which came amid a new escalation in the conflict as President Donald Trump faces growing domestic pressure to end the fighting ahead of November's midterm elections.
ICYMI: What happened in suspected US strike which hit Iran wedding?
At least four people were killed in a suspected US attack that hit a wedding in Iran after Tehran and Washington exchanged the heaviest strikes between them since July.
The Iranian Red Crescent (IRC) has asked the International Criminal Court to investigate the incident, calling for "an independent, impartial, thorough, and effective investigation" due to the "civilian character of the location". Iran has accused the US of "war crimes", but the US maintains that it does not target civilians.
The Independent looks at how the attack took place and what both parties have said about it.
US in turmoil: Trump faces Iran war nightmare as diesel hits record $5.85 and prices threaten to soar
Fuel costs hit an unprecedented high in the U.S. on Friday, with diesel soaring to a record national average of $5.85 a gallon as an ongoing six-month war with Iran continues to disrupt global fuel flows.
Because freight and delivery networks rely heavily on diesel, these rising expenses mean higher transportation costs for a vast array of everyday consumer goods.
Commercial enterprises across multiple sectors are absorbing steeper bills, with several already passing the burden on to buyers through added fees on online orders and packages in the mail. Consequently, shoppers are likely to see increasing sticker shock trickle onto store shelves.

Iranian officials acknowledge in private that US pressure is working
Three senior Iranian sources have told the Reuters news agency that the US campaign to throttle Iran's economy by blockading its oil exports is growing increasingly difficult to withstand.
While Iran's clerical rulers have managed to get around harsh sanctions for decades, the latest US movements have left them in a far more sensitive position, with few remaining channels to secure foreign currency or buy goods, the sources said.
Iran publicly maintains that it has plenty foreign currency reserves and is not meaningfully affected by the US crackdown on sanctions evasion.
The latest measures expanded secondary sanctions that target countries doing business with Iran in a bid to stop it clearing dollar transactions needed for both oil sales and to finance crucial imports of goods and raw materials.
That effort is making Iran's existing sanctions evasion networks - front companies, unregistered tankers and smuggling - too expensive to use, the three senior sources said.
One of the sources said Iran only has another two months' supply of gasoline, which has to be imported due to limited refining capacity.
Araghchi defends Iran over strikes on Jordan
Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi takes to social media to respond to his Jordanian counterpart's recent comments criticising Iran for strikes on Jordan and neighbouring countries.
The Jordanian minister Ayman Safadi said that attacks on his country came within two hours of the start of the war, in February, suggesting the attack was not reactionary.
Araghchi writes: "How much time does the Jordanian Foreign Minister believe Iran should wait before responding to an aggressor that respects neither Arab sovereignty nor Iranian sovereignty?"
He adds: "And is he truly unaware that Arab airspace, lands, and waters were used in the initial American attacks that resulted in the killing of innocent Iranians?"
new_text:
The US and Iran have traded strikes on ships, the latest round of attacks since the conflict flared a week ago after a period of relative calm.
US Central Command, which oversees the nation's military in the Middle East, said it struck three Iranian oil tankers, including one off the coast of Kharg Island, near the nation's oil export hub, after Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched ballistic missiles at two US Navy ships.
Admiral Brad Cooper, head of US Central Command, said: "Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost - taking out three of yours."
The IRGC responded by threatening intensified strikes against US military vessels in the region, and later said it targeted three tankers that Tehran claimed were on unauthorised routes in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as as three US-linked vessels in other areas.
The exchange of attacks followed an escalation in the past week that threatens to deepen a conflict that has continued since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran in February.

UK chancellor warns of tough Budget because of economic impact of Iran war
The Chancellor has warned that the Budget in the autumn could be tough, as US President Donald Trump's war in the Middle East affects the British economy.
John Healey issued the warning amid the leap in Government borrowing earlier this week, reflecting concerns among lenders about the inflationary impact of the US's war with Iran.
Mr Healey also told the Financial Times he would ensure the UK emerges from his first Budget on 28 October with a solid "buffer against uncertainty".
Economists have predicted that the fiscal buffer Rachel Reeves built up in her last budget, through a combination of tax rises and departmental spending cuts, will be squeezed by the inflationary pressures of ongoing global turmoil.
This could limit prime minister Andy Burnham's ambitions to tackle the cost-of-living crisis, and spending plans across his wider agenda for Government.
The chancellor told the FT: "What's happening in the Middle East is hitting inflation, it's hitting growth, it's hitting borrowing costs."
He added: "It's part of a more dangerous world that is more uncertain and it's one of the challenges we have to meet in this country, but have to meet with other [countries]."
Comment: We are now in the age of the Energy Wars
Israeli military says it strikes southern Lebanon after Hezbollah launched drones
The Israeli military said it was striking southern Lebanon early on Sunday in retaliation for Hezbollah firing two drones at Israeli soldiers stationed in a part of the region it has declared a security zone.
The Israeli military had issued an evacuation warning to areas near a building in Arab Salim town in South Lebanon, saying it will strike it as it is used by Hezbollah.
There was no immediate comment from the Iran-backed group.
On Friday, the Israeli military said it struck weapon storage facilities intended to be used by Hezbollah in south Lebanon.
Since 2 March, Israeli strikes have killed more than 4,300 people in Lebanon.
Iranian death row prisoner smuggles out desperate plea to the world: Do not forget about us
From behind the bars of a brutal Iranian prison, a political dissident awaiting execution describes life behind bars - and says the war with the US has made carrying out executions easier for the regime. Alex Croft reports.
A fuel tanker explosion in west Iran kills 11 and injures 7, report cites fault brakes
A fuel tanker exploded in western Iran, killing 11 people and injuring seven others, state media said.
IRNA reported late Saturday that the tanker hit other cars before bursting into flames near a traffic police station close to the Kurdish city of Sanandaj, some 400 kilometers (248 miles) west of the capital, Tehran. The report cited a faulty brake system.
The injured were transferred to hospitals.
In 2018, a similar road accident between a fuel tanker and an intercity passenger bus near Sanandaj killed 15 people and injured four.
Road and traffic accidents annually leave more than 17,000 dead in Iran. Experts blame the high fatality rate on unsafe vehicles, disregard for traffic rules, and inadequate emergency services.
Watch - 'Small potatoes': Trump says Iran conflict isn't a 'big thing' for US
In full: Trump gets testy and calls Iran war 'small potatoes' when pressed on length of fight
President Donald Trump has backed up comments from his vice president and insisted the Iran conflict is a relatively minor operation, rather than a full-on war.
"I call it a military conflict because it's small potatoes for us," the president told reporters in the Oval Office on Friday. "It's not a big thing."
When pressed by Rachel Scott of ABC News about the record-setting deployments of certain service members as part of the fight, the president lashed out, repeatedly asking, "How long were we in Vietnam?"
President Trump claimed the U.S. had successfully stopped Iran from getting a nuclear weapon and alleged U.S. satellite intelligence would spot any future threats from the country the moment they arose. The U.S. had "essentially taken over" Iran, the Republican said.
US carrier Abraham Lincoln departs Thailand after respite visit
The US aircraft carrier Abraham Lincoln left Thailand on Sunday after a five-day port visit, ending a respite from an extended deployment that included operations in the Middle East, the US Navy said.
"We would like to thank the people of Thailand for their incredible hospitality," US Navy Captain Dan Keeler, the Abraham Lincoln's commanding officer, said in a statement.
Naval deployments typically last for six to nine months, but during times of conflict that can be extended.
The nuclear-powered Lincoln, with roughly 5,000 personnel, was involved in the U.S. naval blockade and combat operations in the war with Iran and - according to Democratic lawmakers - set a modern-day record for consecutive days at sea.
Accompanied by other US naval vessels, the Lincoln arrived early on Wednesday in Thailand, the United States' only treaty partner in mainland Southeast Asia, during a visit that Thai officials said would last five days.
Busloads of sailors and Marines wearing civilian clothes, many smiling and waving, started arriving at a hotel in the resort city of Pattaya, about 150 km (93 miles) southeast of Bangkok, shortly after their ships docked.
US and Iran trade strikes
The US and Iran have traded strikes on ships, the latest round of attacks since the conflict flared a week ago after a period of relative calm.
US Central Command, which oversees the nation's military in the Middle East, said it struck three Iranian oil tankers, including one off the coast of Kharg Island, near the nation's oil export hub, after Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched ballistic missiles at two US Navy ships.
Admiral Brad Cooper, head of US Central Command, said: "Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost - taking out three of yours."
The IRGC responded by threatening intensified strikes against US military vessels in the region, and later said it targeted three tankers Tehran that it claimed were on unauthorised routes in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as as three US-linked vessels in other areas.
The exchange of attacks followed an escalation in the past week that threatens to deepen a conflict that has continued since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran in February.
"Do not be deceived by the 'terrorist' U.S. military and refrain from any suspicious movement aimed at passing through unauthorised waterways," the IRGC Navy said in a statement carried on Iranian state TV. "Otherwise, you will be targeted."
Tasnim, the semi-official Iranian news agency, had reported that four US missiles hit a tanker in the area of Kharg's anchorage. Tasnim quoted local sources as saying there were no casualties and the tanker's crew was being evacuated.
No American personnel were harmed, Central Command said.
